transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hello, Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me today. I hope I'm not taking up too much of your time. Um, well, I suppose the main reason I'm here is... well, it's a bit silly, really, but my concentration just hasn't been quite as reliable lately. 

I mean, it's not a huge problem, I can still do my job as a dentist perfectly fine! But, you know, sometimes I'll be reviewing a patient's chart, or even just relaxing at home trying to lay out a watercolor wash, and... I'll realize I've read the same line three times. My mind just sort of drifts off, usually worrying about silly things, little things that could go wrong. It's probably just my age, right? Or maybe I'm just a bit overtired? I hope that makes sense, and that it's the sort of thing you help people with.
Do you find that your worrying is constant or difficult to control, even when there's no immediate reason to be concerned?

Well, I... I suppose "constant" might be a strong word, but... yes, it does feel a bit tricky to turn off sometimes. I try to be rational about it, you know? I try to reason with myself the exact same way I would with a nervous patient in my chair. I'll tell myself, "Everything is fine, there's no need to fret." 

But... well, it's a bit embarrassing to admit, but one little concern just seems to lead right into the next. Before I know it, instead of just letting it go, I'm... I'm checking my emails again, or reviewing my clinical notes for the third time, or asking my wife the same questions just to be sure. It's silly, I know. I really should be better at managing it at my age. Does that... does that sound like the sort of thing you usually hear from people? I don't want to make a mountain out of a molehill.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or worried about a number of different things, even when there isn’t a clear reason to be concerned?

Well, yes, I suppose it's not just one specific thing. It's... it's a bit of a mixed bag, to be honest. I mean, I know it's completely normal to have some concerns as you transition toward retirement, right? 

But... my mind just keeps circling around all sorts of things lately. I'll be perfectly fine, and then suddenly I'm fretting over whether my older patients are being looked after properly by the new associates. Or I'll start second-guessing if the financial handoff for the practice is actually sound, even though my accountant assures me it is. And... well, I suppose sometimes I worry about whether I'll just become completely useless once I'm fully retired. 

It's all very silly, really. I know the worry feels a bit out of proportion, even to me. I should be looking forward to having more time for my watercolors, not stewing over things I can't control. I hope I don't sound completely neurotic saying all that. Is it fairly common for people my age to get a bit spun up about these sorts of transitions?
Do you notice any physical symptoms, like feeling restless, being easily fatigued, or having tense muscles, especially when you're worrying about these things?

Well, I... I don't want to complain too much, because I know getting a bit tired is just part of getting older, isn't it? I wouldn't say I'm pacing the floors or terribly tense, no. But... I suppose I have noticed that by midafternoon, I just feel completely worn out. 

It's a bit embarrassing to admit, really, because I worry it just sounds like laziness... but it's a sort of exhaustion that a nap or a quiet morning just doesn’t seem to fix. Even simple things I usually enjoy, like weeding the garden or just standing at my easel, they just feel so much heavier than they used to. 

I hope I'm not just making excuses for slowing down. Do you think that sort of tiredness is normal when you've got a lot on your mind? I really want to make sure I'm giving you the right information, and I hope I'm not wasting your time with ordinary aches and pains.
Have you noticed any trouble with your sleep lately—like difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up feeling unrested?

Well, I... I suppose my sleep hasn't been absolutely perfect, but I know it's quite common to sleep a bit less as we get older, right? I try not to make too much of a fuss over it. 

But... well, most nights I do get into bed feeling quite tired. It's just that, as soon as the house gets perfectly quiet, I... my brain just seems to turn on. I start replaying all those patient transfers in my head, or going over the money details for the practice again. It's terribly frustrating, because I know I should just rest. And then, even when I do manage to drift off, I'm usually up staring at the ceiling by four or five in the morning. I just wake up feeling like I never really settled at all. 

I feel a bit foolish admitting it, honestly—like I've somehow forgotten how to just go to sleep like a normal person. Is it... is it fairly typical for people to have their sleep disrupted like this when they've got retirement on their minds? I really don't want to sound like I'm whining about a few lost hours, I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture.

Have you ever experienced sudden episodes where you feel an intense wave of fear or discomfort that comes on quickly, like your heart starts racing, you feel short of breath, or like something terrible is going to happen?

Oh, goodness, no. I... I don't think I've ever had anything quite like that. My heart doesn't race, and I can always catch my breath just fine. It's really more of a... a quiet, constant buzzing of worry in the background, rather than a sudden wave of fear. 

I hope that's alright? I mean, I certainly don't want to sound like I'm dismissing your question at all. It's just that I haven't experienced those sudden, intense feelings you're describing. Is it... is it a bad thing that I don't have those? I just want to make sure I'm giving you exactly what you need to figure this all out, and I hope I'm not being unhelpful or difficult by saying no.

Do you find yourself especially anxious or worried in social situations, such as when you're meeting new people, speaking in front of others, or even just having a conversation with colleagues or patients?

Oh, no, not at all. I... I hope it doesn't sound like I'm just being contrary, but talking to people has always been quite easy for me. I suppose when you've been a dentist as long as I have, making small talk and keeping people comfortable just becomes second nature, doesn't it? 

So, no, chatting with patients or the staff at the clinic, or even meeting someone new... that doesn't really bother me. I've always felt quite comfortable in those situations. 

Is... is that alright? I mean, I know you're asking for a reason, and I'd hate to think I'm missing something you're looking for, or making your job harder by not having these things. I just want to be completely honest so I don't lead you down the wrong path. Am I doing okay with these questions?
Do you ever feel especially anxious or worried when you're away from home or separated from people you care about, like your wife or family?

Oh, no. I... I wouldn't say that's an issue for me. I mean, my wife and I are quite independent, and with the practice, I've always had to be away for long hours anyway. So, being apart from her or the rest of the family doesn't really trigger anything... unusual for me. 

I actually think I handle being away from home quite well. I... I hope that's the sort of answer you're looking for? I know you're trying to cover all the bases, and I really appreciate how thorough you're being. I just want to make sure I'm not... well, frustrating you by saying no to so many of these things. I'm trying my best to give you the clearest picture possible. Am I still being helpful?
Do you feel that these worries and the way they affect your concentration or energy are significantly interfering with your ability to do the things you need or want to do each day?

Well... I suppose... I really don't want to make a mountain out of a molehill, but... yes, I think it is interfering a bit. If I'm being completely honest—and I want to make sure I'm giving you the right information—I’ve actually had to slow down and postpone some parts of the retirement handoff at the clinic. 

I just... I keep second-guessing my decisions, and I end up losing so much time during the day trying to get things perfectly sorted. And... well, even at home, my painting and my gardening just don’t feel as manageable as they used to. I just can't seem to muster the focus or energy for them right now. 

I feel a little embarrassed admitting that, to be honest. A grown man should be able to handle his own retirement and his hobbies, shouldn't he? I hope I'm not sounding too... incapable or weak by saying all this. I just want to make sure I'm giving you exactly what you need. Does that answer your question alright?
Have these feelings of worry, trouble concentrating, and low energy been happening most days, and have they been going on for several months now?

Well, yes... I suppose it has been a while. I... I really hate to admit how long I've let this drag on without getting a handle on it. It's... it's been going on since I started the formal retirement process. Which, well, that was about a year and three months ago now. 

And, yes, it does feel like it's most days. I just... I kept thinking I'd turn a corner, you know? That once I got the next piece of paperwork signed or the next transition meeting out of the way, I'd feel like my old self again. I feel quite foolish letting it go on for over a year like this. I should have been able to manage it better. 

I hope it's alright that I waited so long to talk to someone about it. I know doctors always prefer to catch these things early... I'm not making things too difficult by bringing this to you so late in the game, am I?
Do you ever worry excessively about having a physical symptom like a racing heart or shortness of breath, even if it doesn’t happen suddenly or intensely?

Oh, no... no, I don't think so. I mean, I'm getting older, so occasionally I might notice my heart beating a little faster if I've been rushing around, but... I don't really worry about it. I certainly don't obsess over it or anything like that. 

I try to stay fairly sensible about my health. Being a dentist, I suppose I have a bit of a medical background, so I try not to let every little ache or pain send me into a panic. I hope that's the right way to handle it? I just... I don't want to come across as a hypochondriac or someone who complains about every little thing. I'm trying to give you the most accurate picture I can... does that make sense?
Do you ever feel especially anxious or upset when thinking about being separated from your wife or other loved ones, even if it's just for a short time?

Oh, no... no, I wouldn't say that at all. My wife and I, well... we've always been quite comfortable doing our own things. I mean, I love her dearly, of course! I really hope saying that doesn't make me sound cold or, you know, unattached. 

It's just that if she goes out of town for a few days to visit family, or even if she's just out running errands for the afternoon, I don't get upset or worry about the separation itself. I think we have a pretty normal, healthy independence in that regard... at least, I hope we do. 

Is that what you were asking about? I just want to make sure I'm understanding your questions properly so I can give you exactly what you need.

Do you ever feel especially anxious or self-conscious when you're being observed or evaluated, such as during public speaking, performing a task in front of others, or even in situations like playing a game with friends?

Well, no, I can't say that I do. As a dentist, I've actually spent most of my career with people watching my hands work—patients, hygienists, dental assistants. I suppose if I got nervous every time someone was observing me, I wouldn't have been very good at my job! 

So, no, I don't really get stage fright or worry about people evaluating me during a task. Even just playing a round of golf or cards with the guys, I'm perfectly comfortable. 

I hope it's alright that I'm saying no to some of these. I want to make sure I'm giving you the right information... I'm not being too difficult, am I? I just want to be as honest as possible so you have exactly what you need to help me.
Do you ever feel especially anxious or upset when thinking about being separated from your wife or other loved ones, even if it's just for a short time?

Oh, um... I think you might have actually just asked me about this one a moment ago? About being separated from my wife? Or maybe I'm misunderstanding and you mean something slightly different this time... please let me know if I am! 

But yes, just to reiterate, no, I really don't get upset or anxious about that at all. We're very comfortable being apart for errands or when she goes out of town. 

I hope I didn't give the wrong impression earlier? I'm so sorry if my first answer was confusing or if I didn't explain it properly... I can certainly try to elaborate more if you need me to? I'm really just trying to be as helpful and accurate as I can for you.
Do you ever feel especially anxious or upset when thinking about being separated from your wife or other loved ones, even if it's just for a short time?

Oh, my... um, I am so sorry, but I believe that might be the exact same question again? 

I really hope I'm not doing something wrong here... Have I been answering poorly? I feel just awful if I'm not giving you the information you're looking for, or if I'm somehow making your job harder today. I must be doing a terrible job explaining myself!

But, um, yes, just to be completely honest with you... I still don't have any anxiety at all about being apart from my wife or anyone else. We really are quite fine doing our own things. 

I really hope it's okay that my answer is still no. Is there... is there a specific way you'd like me to answer these? I just want to make absolutely sure I'm doing this right for you.

Do you ever feel especially anxious or self-conscious when you're the center of attention in non-professional situations, such as giving a toast at a family gathering or speaking up in a small group setting?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I don't think so. I've given a few toasts at weddings and anniversaries over the years, and I always just try to keep things light and friendly. I suppose anyone gets a tiny bit of butterflies right before they speak, but it's nothing that really bothers me or makes me overly self-conscious. 

I usually just focus on making sure everyone is having a good time and that I'm not taking up too much of their evening. I really hope that's an okay answer? I know I keep saying no to some of these things, and I just want to make sure I'm not coming across as uncooperative or anything. I'm really trying my best to give you a clear picture of how I am.
Do you ever feel especially anxious or overwhelmed when thinking about specific upcoming events or changes related to your retirement?

Well, um... yes. I suppose I do. I hope I don't sound ungrateful or foolish, because retirement is supposed to be this wonderful milestone, right? But... my mind just keeps circling around all sorts of things lately. 

I try to keep a brave face about it, but I catch myself constantly fretting over whether my old patients are really being looked after properly by the new team. And, um, I worry if the practice handoff is entirely financially sound... and, to be perfectly honest with you, I worry a lot about whether I’ll just become completely useless once I’m fully retired and not practicing dentistry anymore. 

I know I shouldn't let it get to me so much, and the amount of worry really feels out of proportion even to me... I feel a bit silly even admitting it out loud to you. I just hope it's okay that I feel a little overwhelmed by all that? Does that sound like an alright or normal reaction to you?
Do you ever feel anxious about experiencing physical symptoms, like dizziness or chest tightness, even if they don’t lead to a serious problem?

Oh, um... no, not really. I mean, I don't think I worry about things like that very much. I try to stay fairly active, you know, and I've always been pretty healthy overall, so I don't really get too worked up about little aches or pains. 

If I ever felt a little dizzy or something, I think I'd just sit down and drink some water. I certainly wouldn't want to make a fuss over it or bother anyone if it wasn't a real emergency. 

I hope that's an okay answer? I know you're trying to be very thorough, and I really appreciate how careful you're being with all these questions. I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of information... am I doing alright with this one?
Do you ever worry that you might experience sudden physical symptoms like a racing heart or dizziness, even if they haven't caused you serious problems?

Um, no, I... I don't think so. That sounds a bit like what you just asked, actually, unless I'm misunderstanding? 

Like I was saying, I really don't tend to fret over my heart rate or feeling lightheaded or anything of that sort. I try not to be the type of person who focuses too much on every little physical sensation, you know? I think it's better to just keep moving forward and not make a big deal out of every little twinge. 

I hope I'm understanding your question right? I'd hate to be giving you the same answer if you were looking for something different. I just want to make sure I'm being helpful. Is it alright that I don't really have those kinds of worries?
